summary.text: The proof rewrites each summand as \(\binom Nj\,N^{\overline j}\), so the shorter sum can be extended by zero binomial terms and compared term by term. The rising factorial is unchanged modulo \(k\) under \(N\mapsto N+k\), while Vandermonde’s identity shows the binomial-factor change is divisible by \(k\): every nonconstant term contains \(\binom{k}{i}n^{\overline i}\), divisible by \(k\) via \(i\binom{k}{i}=k\binom{k-1}{i-1}\) and \(i\mid n^{\overline i}\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(N)=N![x^N]\frac{e^x}{(1-x)^N}\qquad(N\ge 0).
\]
We prove that for every pair of nonnegative integers \(n,k\),
\[
a(n+k)\equiv a(n)\pmod{k}.
\]
Here congruence modulo \(0\) has its usual divisibility meaning: \(u\equiv v\pmod 0\) means \(0\mid u-v\), hence means \(u=v\).

First we put the sequence into the finite-sum form used in the argument. For \(N\ge 1\), the standard power-series expansions
\[
e^x=\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{x^r}{r!},
\qquad
(1-x)^{-N}=\sum_{s\ge0}\binom{N+s-1}{s}x^s
\]
give
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
&=N!\sum_{r+s=N}\frac1{r!}\binom{N+s-1}{s}\\
&=\sum_{s=0}^N \frac{N!}{(N-s)!}\binom{N+s-1}{s}\\
&=\sum_{s=0}^N \binom Ns\binom{N+s-1}{s}s!.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(N=0\), the defining coefficient is \([x^0]e^x=1\), and the same finite sum consists only of its \(s=0\) term and also equals \(1\). Thus, for every \(N\ge0\),
\[
a(N)=\sum_{j=0}^N \binom Nj\binom{N+j-1}{j}j!,
\tag{1}
\]
where at \(N=j=0\) the second binomial coefficient is understood as \(1\). Equivalently, one may write it as \(\binom{(N+j)-1}{j}\), with truncated natural-number subtraction; this also gives \(\binom00=1\) in the exceptional case.

Introduce the rising factorial
\[
N^{\overline j}=N(N+1)\cdots(N+j-1),
\qquad N^{\overline0}=1.
\]
For all \(N,j\ge0\),
\[
N^{\overline j}=j!\binom{N+j-1}{j}.
\tag{2}
\]
For \(N\ge1\) this is the usual factorial identity. If \(N=0\) and \(j>0\), both sides vanish, while if \(N=j=0\), both sides are \(1\). Consequently, if
\[
g(N,j)=\binom Nj N^{\overline j},
\tag{3}
\]
then (1) becomes
\[
a(N)=\sum_{j=0}^N g(N,j).
\tag{4}
\]
Moreover, \(g(N,j)=0\) whenever \(j>N\), because then \(\binom Nj=0\). We may therefore extend the upper limit in (4) to any integer at least \(N\).

We next prove the key termwise assertion
\[
k\mid g(n+k,j)-g(n,j)
\qquad\text{for every }n,k,j\ge0.
\tag{5}
\]
The proof has two parts, one for the rising factorial and one for the binomial coefficient.

First,
\[
(n+k)^{\overline j}\equiv n^{\overline j}\pmod{k}.
\tag{6}
\]
Indeed,
\[
(n+k)^{\overline j}=\prod_{t=0}^{j-1}(n+k+t),
\qquad
n^{\overline j}=\prod_{t=0}^{j-1}(n+t),
\]
and corresponding factors are congruent modulo \(k\). Multiplying these congruences proves (6). This includes \(j=0\), when both products are empty and equal to \(1\). Thus
\[
k\mid (n+k)^{\overline j}-n^{\overline j}.
\tag{7}
\]

For the second part we will show
\[
k\mid \left(\binom{n+k}{j}-\binom nj\right)n^{\overline j}.
\tag{8}
\]
We first establish an elementary absorption divisibility. For every \(i>0\),
\[
k\mid \binom ki n^{\overline i}.
\tag{9}
\]
If \(k=0\), then \(i>0\) implies \(\binom0i=0\), so the product in (9) is zero and the assertion is true even in the divisibility-by-zero sense. Now suppose \(k>0\). The product of \(i\) consecutive integers
\[
n^{\overline i}=n(n+1)\cdots(n+i-1)
\]
is divisible by \(i\). One direct way to see this is that it is in fact divisible by \(i!\): for \(n>0\), identity (2) writes it as \(i!\binom{n+i-1}{i}\), and for \(n=0\) it is zero. Hence write
\[
n^{\overline i}=iT
\]
for some integer \(T\). The standard binomial identity
\[
i\binom ki=k\binom{k-1}{i-1}
\tag{10}
\]
then gives
\[
\binom ki n^{\overline i}
 =\binom ki\,iT
 =k\binom{k-1}{i-1}T,
\]
which proves (9). Identity (10) remains valid when \(i>k\), since the relevant binomial coefficients then vanish, so no additional range restriction on \(i\) is needed.

We now apply Vandermonde’s identity:
\[
\binom{n+k}{j}
 =\sum_{i+r=j}\binom ki\binom nr.
\tag{11}
\]
The summand with \(i=0\) is \(\binom nj\). Therefore
\[
\binom{n+k}{j}-\binom nj
 =\sum_{\substack{i+r=j\\i>0}}\binom ki\binom nr.
\tag{12}
\]
Multiply this equation by \(n^{\overline j}\). For each pair \(i,r\) occurring in the sum, so that \(i+r=j\), the rising factorial splits as
\[
n^{\overline j}
 =n^{\overline i}(n+i)^{\overline r}.
\tag{13}
\]
Thus the corresponding summand on the right of (12), after multiplication by \(n^{\overline j}\), is
\[
\binom ki\binom nr n^{\overline j}
 =\left(\binom ki n^{\overline i}\right)
   \left(\binom nr (n+i)^{\overline r}\right).
\tag{14}
\]
Because \(i>0\), the first parenthesis in (14) is divisible by \(k\) by (9). Hence every summand is divisible by \(k\), and so is their sum. This proves (8).

We can now prove (5). By adding and subtracting
\(\binom{n+k}{j}n^{\overline j}\), we have the exact identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
g(n+k,j)-g(n,j)
={}&\binom{n+k}{j}
 \left((n+k)^{\overline j}-n^{\overline j}\right)\\
&+\left(\binom{n+k}{j}-\binom nj\right)n^{\overline j}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]
The first term on the right is divisible by \(k\) by (7), and the second is divisible by \(k\) by (8). Their sum is therefore divisible by \(k\), proving the termwise congruence (5).

It remains only to sum these congruences over a common range. Formula (4) gives
\[
a(n+k)=\sum_{j=0}^{n+k}g(n+k,j).
\tag{16}
\]
On the other hand, because \(g(n,j)=0\) for every \(j>n\), we may extend the sum for \(a(n)\) to the same endpoint:
\[
a(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n+k}g(n,j).
\tag{17}
\]
Subtracting (17) from (16),
\[
a(n+k)-a(n)
 =\sum_{j=0}^{n+k}\bigl(g(n+k,j)-g(n,j)\bigr).
\tag{18}
\]
Every summand on the right is divisible by \(k\) by (5), so the entire sum is divisible by \(k\). Hence
\[
a(n+k)\equiv a(n)\pmod{k}.
\]

This also covers \(k=0\): in that case each difference in (5), and directly the left side of the desired congruence, is zero because \(n+k=n\). Therefore the result holds for all nonnegative integers \(n\) and \(k\).
